newsitem.title: USA: Midwest Fed mulls economic threat of big hog farms.
newsitem.headline: Midwest Fed mulls economic threat of big hog farms.

text.p: Changes in U.S. pork production due to the rapid rise of hog "mega farms" present a stark challenge to the Midwest's traditional dominance in the $30 billion pork industry, the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago said in a new study.

The study, "Industrialization in hog production: implications for Midwest agriculture," said the social and environmental problems associated with "mega" producers with 2,000 or more hogs at one location had fed public resistance in the bank's five-state district that had cost the region market share in the 1990's and looked set to continue.

"The hog production and processing models and standards that have come about with the industrialization of recent years present a rather foreboding picture for the typical family farm concept of Midwest hog production," said the study, authored by Gary Benjamin, a Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago vice president and economic adviser.

"The standards set by the largest hog producers now suggest that some 50 producers could account for all the hogs needed in the United States. Moreover, the standards set by new, state-of-the-art packing plants suggest that fewer than 12 plants could process all the country's hogs," it said.
"If the restructuring process goes that far, many rural communities will be affected," the study concluded.
The Chicago Fed's district includes Michigan, Wisconsin, Iowa, Illinois and Indiana, the last three traditionally among the top five states in U.S. pork production and processing.

The rise of "mega farms" with 2,000-plus hogs has been most notable in North Carolina and Missouri. North Carolina, seventh in hog inventory in 1990 with 2.7 million head, surged past Illinois in 1993 as the second biggest hog state after Iowa. At the end of 1995, North Carolina had 8.2 million hogs, Illinois 4.8 million and Iowa 13.4 million, the study said.
While hog numbers in North Carolina and Missouri more than doubled in 1991-1995, hog numbers in the Chicago Fed's five district states fell three percent, the study said.
Five other states not traditionally known for hog production -- Colorado, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Utah and Wyoming -- recorded a 300 percent rise in hogs in the period.

The study said corporate integration and specialization in hog production had so boosted productivity by economies of scale, genetics, breeding, medicine and marketing that family farm suppliers were being inexorably replaced. Some 183,000 hog farms were operating at end-1995, down 206,000 from 1985.
It said the key obstacle to the Midwest retaining its lead in hog production and, in turn, pork processing remains environmental issues, especially waste treatment and odors.

"Observers have suggested the recent success of states on the western fringe of the Corn Belt in attracting mega producers is due largely to the less intense environmental concerns in those areas as compared to the more populous rural areas of the Midwest," the study said.
Lower land costs and population densities in those areas also made it easier to site a large hog operation at a safe distance from neighbors, the study said.

"Another key issue for the Midwest is the likelihood that the economic activity of pork packing and processing will follow any geographical shift in hog production," the study said, noting the Midwest currently had "an even larger share in hog processing than in hog raising."
The five district states now account for about 48 percent of the annual $11 billion in live hog sales, it said.
